topics.title: k MATHCOUNTS 2011 National Sprint #22, #27, #29, #30 Geometry
topics.text:
I recently did the MATHCOUNTS 2011 National Sprint Round, and had some questions on a few geometry problems.



22.) Circle $O$ has radius $10$ units. Point $P$ is on radius $OQ$ and $OP = 6$ units. How many different chords containing $p$, including the diameter, have integer lengths?



27.) Circle $O$ has radius $8$ unites and circle $P$ has radius $2$ units. The circles are externally tangent to each other at point $Q$. Segment $TS$  is tangent to both circle $O$ and circle $P$ at points $T$ and $S$, respectively. What is the length of segment $OS$? Express your answer in simplest radical form.



29.) In pentagon $ABCDE$, $BC = CD = DE = 2$ units, $\angle E$ is a right angle, and $m\angle B  = m\angle C = m\angle D = 135$. The length of segment $AE$ can be expressed in simplest radical form as $a+2\sqrt{b}$ units. What is the value of $a+b$?



30.) In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 12$ units and $AC = 9$ units. Point $D$ is on segment $BC$ so that $BD:DC = 2:1$. If $AD = 6$ units, what is the length of segment $BC$? Express your answer in simplest radical form.



Answers22.) $8$ chords

27.) $8\sqrt{2}$ units

29.) $6$

30.) $3\sqrt{33}$ units




Any tips, hints, or solutions are appreciated! Please stay on topic, so this thread doesn't get locked.



Thanks,

zac15SCASD

topics.title: k Algebra Sprint
topics.text:
Hello,

I would like to start an  Algebra Sprint. Here are the rules:

•	Please number your problems and solutions so that people will know which problem/solution you are referring to.

•	This sprint will end after the $50^{th}$ problem.

•	Please use the "hide" tags for your problems and solutions like this:

*(Please note the quotes around the Problem/Solution Title, they are mandatory.)

Problem/Solution Title with Number.Problem/Solution goes here


•	I will post the first problem. Then someone else can post a full solution to my problem (remember to use the "hide" tags and numbering!) in addition to posting a new problem. If you don't have a new problem, you can always use Google! But make sure to cite the source you used to get the problem.

•	Why is it important to useYou should use the "hide" tags so that people won't have to have the solutions staring at them right in the face. When the solution is easily accessible, people will have a tendency to look at it right away if they can't do the problem on the first try, and if you do that, you aren't learning at all.



Additionally, you should also number your problems so that referencing different problems can be much less problematic.






•	***IMPORTANT***

Above all, remember the level of this sprint, this is the Algebra Sprint so try not to make the name of this Sprint  start deceiving others like this MOEMS marathon is...(I think it's getting way too advanced for MOEMS). Anyways, just remember to keep the problems at a $5^{th}$ to $8^{th}$ grade normal math level but the problems can (and should) challenge the younger portion of this community.



Here's the first problem:

Problem #1Find the sum of the Arithmetic Progression.

topics.title: k Defining Pi
topics.text:
Pi is the ratio of the circumference (perimeter) of a given circle to its diameter. It is approximately equal to 3.141592653. The number pi is one of the most important constants in all of mathematics and appears in some of the most surprising places, such as in the sum $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{6}$. Some common fractional approximations for pi are $\frac{22}{7} \approx 3.14285$ and $\frac{355}{113} \approx 3.1415929$.

The number pi often shows up in problems in number theory, particularly algebraic number theory. For example, many class number formulae involve pi.

$\pi$ can be calculated in several ways, and it can also be approximated. One way to approximate $\pi$ is to inscribe a unit circle in a square of side length 2. Using a computer, random points are placed inside the square. Because the area of the circle is $\pi$, and the area of the square is 4, the ratio of the amount of points inside the circle to the total number of points approximates $\frac{\pi}{4}$. This can simply be multiplied by 4 to approximate $\pi$.

One formula for pi is $4\left( \sum_{i = 0}^\infty (-1)^i \left(\frac{1}{2n+1}\right)\right)$. This can be computed to the desired degree of accuracy.

Letting $\theta = \pi$ in Euler's identity gives $e^{\pi i} + 1 = 0$, which is considered to be one of the most beautiful results in mathematics since it involves five of the greatest constants: e, pi, i, 1, and 0.

In this section we'll outline the Beukers proof that $\pi$ is not Liouvillian, i.e., that $\left|\pi-\frac pq\right|\ge \frac 1{q^M}$ for large $q$ with some fixed positive $M$. The best known value of $M$ is currently (June, 1993) $M=8.02$ and is due to Hata. This article can be read right after its parent article rational approximation of famous numbers, but an unexperienced reader may prefer to read the proof that ln 2 is not Liouvillian first.

Note that if $x$ is Liouvillian, then so is any rational multiple of any positive integer power of $x$ (this is a simple exercise we leave to the reader), so, it will suffice to show that $\frac{\pi^2}6$ is not Liouvillian.

$\frac{\pi^2}6=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac 1{m^2}$Consider the integrals $I(k,\ell):=\iint_{(0,1)\times(0,1)}\frac {x^ky^\ell}{1-xy}\,dx\,dy$. Expanding $\frac 1{1-xy}=\sum_{j=0}^\infty x^jy^j$ and integrating term by term, we get $I(k,\ell)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac1{(k+j+1)(\ell+j+1)}.$

If $k=\ell$, we get the sum of all inverse squares starting with $\frac 1{(k+1)^2}$, so in this case,

$I(k,\ell)=\frac {\pi^2}{6}-\frac 1{1^2}-\frac 1{2^2}-\dots-\frac 1{k^2}.$

On the other hand, if $k>\ell$, we get

$I(k,\ell)=\frac 1{k-\ell}\sum_{j=0}^\infty\left[\frac 1{\ell+j+1}-\frac {1}{k+j+1}\right]=\frac 1{k-\ell}\left[\frac 1{\ell+1}+\frac 1{\ell+2}+\dots+\frac 1k\right]$

Similarly, if $\ell>k$, we get

$I(k,\ell)=\frac 1{\ell-k}\left[\frac 1{k+1}+\frac 1{k+2}+\dots+\frac 1\ell\right]$

Let now $D_n$ be the least common multiple of $1,2,\dots,n$. It follows immediately from the above formulae for $I(k,\ell)$ that for every polynomial $R(x,y)$ with integer coefficients whose degree in both $x$ and $y$ does not exceed $n$, we have

$D_n^2\iint_{(0,1)\times(0,1)}\frac {R(x,y)}{1-xy}\,dx\,dy=P_n-Q_n\frac{\pi^2}{6}$ where $P_n,Q_n\in \mathbb Z$.

The trick is to choose a polynomial $R(x,y)$ that makes the integral very small. We put

$R(x,y)=\frac 1{n!}(1-y)^n\left(\frac d{dx}\right)^n [x^n(1-x)^n].$

Note that $R(x,y)$ has integer coefficients as a product of two polynomials with integer coefficients.

Since the largest possible power of a given prime $p\le n$ that can divide one of the numbers $1,2,\dots,n$ is $\left\lfloor\frac{\log n}{\log p}\right\rfloor$ where $\lfloor\cdot\rfloor$ is the floor function, we have $D_n=\prod_{p\mathrm{\  prime,}\,p\le n}p^{\left\lfloor\frac{\log n}{\log p}\right\rfloor}\approx n^{\pi(n)}$ where $\pi(n)$ is the number of primes not exceeding $n$. According to the prime number theorem, we have $\pi(n)\approx \frac n{\log n}$, so $D_n\approx e^n.$ (The exact meaning of the $\approx$ sign here is that, as $n\to\infty$, the ratio of the $n$-th roots of the left and the right sides tends to $1$. Note also that we need the full strength of the prime number theorem here. The elementary Chebyshev's estimate $D_n\le n^{\sqrt n}\cdot 4^n$ is no longer sufficient).Integrating $n$ times by parts with respect to $x$, we see that our integral equals $\iint_{(0,1)\times(0,1)}\left[\frac {x(1-x)y(1-y)}{1-xy}\right]^n\,\frac {dx\,dy}{1-xy}$. We want to estimate $\max_{0<x,y<1}\frac {x(1-x)y(1-y)}{1-xy}$. The first remark is that it is attained on the diagonal $x=y$. It becomes clear if we rewrite the fraction as $\frac {xy(1-x-y+xy)}{1-xy}$ and recall that for a fixed product $xy$ the minimum of the sum $x+y$ is achieved when $x=y$. So, we need to find the maximum of $\frac {x^2(1-x)^2}{1-x^2}=\frac {x^2(1-x)}{1+x}$ over the interval $(0,1)$. Taking the logarithmic derivative and solving the resulting quadratic equation $\frac 2x-\frac 1{1-x}-\frac 1{1+x}=0$, we see that the maximum is attained at the point $x=\frac{\sqrt 5-1}{2}$ and equals $\frac{5\sqrt 5-11}2$. It means that the integral does not exceed  $\left(\frac{5\sqrt 5-11}2\right)^n I(0,0)\approx \left(\frac{5\sqrt 5-11}2\right)^n$.

On the other hand, to estimate the integral from below, it suffices to notice that the integrand is at least $\frac 4{81}$ for $\frac 1 3\le x,y\le\frac 2 3$. Thus, the integral is not much less than $\left(\frac 4{81}\right)^n$.

The miracle that makes the proof work is that $e^2\cdot\frac{5\sqrt 5-11}2$ is strictly less than $1$ (just check it on your calculator or prove it by hand yourself). Thus, for large $n$, the whole product $D_n^2\iint_{(0,1)\times(0,1)}\frac {R(x,y)}{1-xy}\,dx\,dy$ can be estimated from above and from below by the $n$-th powers of some constants strictly between $0$ and $1$. Using the main theorem from the parent article, we see that it remains only to show that $Q_n$ grow not faster than some geometric progression.Note that $Q_n$ is just minus the product of $D_n^2$, which grows like $e^{2n}$ and the sum of the coefficients of the polynomial $R(x,y)$ at the products $x^ky^k$ with $k=0,\dots,n$. It follows that $|Q_n|$ does not exceed the sum of coefficients of $(1-y)^n$, which is $2^n$, times the maximal coefficient of $\frac 1{n!}\left(\frac d{dx}\right)^n[x^n(1-x)^n]$. But even the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients of this polynomial does not exceed  $8^n$. So $|Q_n|$ grows not much faster than $(16e^2)^n$ and we are done.

SourceAops Wiki

topics.title: A question relating surface area and volume
topics.text:
Hi, my brother was having issues with this problem (there is an official solution but not the steps), and I managed to solve it by reducing the solution space and using good guessing. I'm wondering if it's possible to solve this algebraically, or if there is a better way, since my method still takes a bit too long.



The problem is:



The surface area of a closed jewelry box is 832 $cm^2$. The measures (in $cm$) of its sides are integers and they form an arithmetic sequence.

What is the volume of the box (in $cm^3$)?



I solved it by showing that, calling the 3 sides x, x+a, x+2a:

1.The Surface area equation reduces to 416 = 3x^2 + 6xa + 2a^2

2.This implies x^2 is even, so x is even as well since x is an integer

3. The dividing by 2, 208 = 3x^2/2 + 3xa + a^2

4. This implies a^2 is even, so a is even since a is also an integer

5. Using these two facts, I guess and checked adding the pairwise combinations of the last digits of my guesses, to see if they add to 6 (multiplying by 2 makes it the last digit 2 of the surface area sum). The ones that satisfy this condition, I then do the full calculation to see if the surface area is indeed 832. Turns out, it is 8, 12, 16 as the solution (didn't take long to find this pattern, since the the conditions I found did reduce the problem greatly).



However, it seems my method is still quite long, and I was wondering if there are more elegant methods?

topics.title: Combinations (and casework?)
topics.text:
If six people randomly sit down at a table with six chairs, and they do not notice that there are name tags marking assigned seats, what is the probability that exactly three of them will sit in the seat he or she was assigned? Express your answer as a common fraction.



Source: 2015 Nationals Sprint #22

I don't get itThis is my original solution:

There is a $1/6$ chance of the first person sitting in the correct seat. Then, there is a $1/5$ chance of the second person sitting in the correct seat, and similarly for the 3rd person. For the 4th person,

there is a 2/3 chance of him/her sitting in the wrong seat, and for the 5th person, there is a 1/2 chance of him/her sitting in the wrong seat. Multiply the product of all that by $\binom{6}{3}$ since the correct and wrong people are interchangeable. You get 1/18, which seems to be the correct answer according to the answer key.



However, let's say that person 4 sits in person 5's seat, which has a 1/3 probability. Then, person 5 has a 100% chance of sitting in the wrong seat. And then person 6 has to sit in the correct seat, which does not satisfy the required conditions. The probability of this case happening is $1/6*1/5*1/4*1/3*\binom{6}{3}$, which is equal to $1/18$. Therefore, the answer is $1/18-1/18=0$? What am I doing wrong?

topics.title: How To Get Motivated :)
topics.text:
Hey AoPS members!

So I'm sure that most of us are off of competition season right now, like for AMC and Mathcounts, but when it's a few months away from competition, it's good to know how to get motivated again.  Here are my tips to get motivated for math competitions:



1. Enjoy What You're Doing: To work as hard and efficiently as possible, you have to like what you're doing to look forward to it.  For example, if you hate worksheets but like to play games, you won't want to learn through dozens of worksheets.  Look up a Jeopardy game for the topic you want to learn and you're more likely to work harder.



2. Think of the End Result: In order to do the best possible, you must practice, practice, practice!  You can't expect results unless you put the work and effort in.  If you remember this, it will help greatly.



3. List Your Goals: This one may sound dumb, but it helps drastically.  Write down a list of realistic goals you have and don't stop until you've accomplished all of them.  It's very satisfying to check things off your list, too.  :D



4. Just Start! :): This is the most straight-forward step.  If nothing is motivating you, set a timer, and just work until the timer is gone.  This works every time, because humans are programmed to finish tasks, so you'll want to work even more after the timer.



I really hope these tips helped get some of you guys motivated! This is my first "forum" that I've created, so if I did anything wrong, you can just tell me.  Thank you!
